title: Designing cooler streets
content:
A. On a summer afternoon, two streets in the same neighbourhood can feel surprisingly different. One may be lined with mature trees, while the other consists largely of exposed paving. This contrast has encouraged urban planners to look beyond city-wide temperature averages. The following account describes an invented pilot project in the fictional city of Bellford. It illustrates the kinds of choices a council might face when trying to make walking more comfortable during hot weather.

B. Bellford's planners began by measuring surface temperatures along twelve walking routes. Measurements were taken at the same time on several clear afternoons, using the same type of instrument. The team also recorded the amount of shade and counted pedestrians. They found that uncovered paving was often much warmer than shaded paving nearby. However, these measurements described the temperature of the ground, not the temperature of the air. The distinction mattered because a lower surface reading did not, by itself, show how comfortable a pedestrian would feel.

C. Planting trees appeared to offer a promising long-term response. Their leaves block some sunlight, and water released through the leaves can help cool the surrounding environment. Yet a newly planted tree provides far less shade than a mature one. In narrow streets, roots may also compete for space with underground pipes. The council therefore rejected the idea of planting identical trees along every route. Instead, specialists selected species according to the space, soil and water available at each site.

D. Where trees could not be planted immediately, the council installed temporary shade structures near bus stops. These could be moved if travel patterns changed. A lighter paving material was tested on a small square as well. Although it reflected more sunlight than the original surface, some residents reported uncomfortable glare. The pilot showed why a material's technical performance should be considered alongside people's experience of using the space. No single design was adopted as a solution for the entire city.

E. To understand these experiences, volunteers interviewed people who regularly walked along the trial routes. Older residents often placed particular value on benches where they could rest in the shade. Parents with young children emphasised safe crossings. Several shop owners wanted changes that would keep entrances visible and allow deliveries to continue. These responses did not replace the temperature measurements; they added information that the instruments could not provide.

F. After the first summer, the council decided to extend the trial for another year. It had not yet collected enough evidence to determine which combination of measures offered the best value over time. Maintenance costs, tree survival and patterns of use would all be monitored. The planners concluded that a cooler street should be judged as a place people use, rather than solely as a surface with a lower temperature.

questions.question: The team measured temperatures on twelve walking routes.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explicitly gives the number of routes as twelve. The statement agrees with the passage.
questions.evidence: Bellford's planners began by measuring surface temperatures along twelve walking routes.
questions.trap: Do not confuse the number of routes with the number of measurement days.
questions.tip: Find the specific quantity and the noun it describes.

questions.question: The instruments were used to measure the temperature of the air.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says the readings measured the ground rather than the air, so there is a direct contradiction.
questions.evidence: However, these measurements described the temperature of the ground, not the temperature of the air.
questions.trap: The familiar phrase 'temperature of the air' appears in the text, but it is negated.
questions.tip: Read the entire sentence, including words such as 'not'.

questions.question: The temporary shade structures were more expensive than planting trees.
questions.explanation: The text describes the structures and says they could be moved. It does not compare their cost with the cost of trees.
questions.evidence: Where trees could not be planted immediately, the council installed temporary shade structures near bus stops.
questions.trap: A plausible cost comparison is still unsupported if no cost evidence is given.
questions.tip: Choose NOT GIVEN when the required comparison is absent.

questions.question: Why did the council avoid planting identical trees along every route?
options: A. Residents preferred streets without trees.
B. Different sites had different growing conditions and space.
C. All underground pipes had to be removed first.
D. Mature trees produce less shade than young trees.
questions.explanation: Species were selected to match each site's space, soil and water. The other options either contradict the passage or add information it does not contain.
questions.evidence: Instead, specialists selected species according to the space, soil and water available at each site.
questions.trap: The mention of pipes does not mean that all pipes needed removal.
questions.tip: Prefer the option that explains the decision as a whole.

questions.question: Complete with ONE WORD from the passage: Some residents found the lighter paving uncomfortable because of its _____.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D directly identifies glare as the drawback reported by residents. Use the noun from the text and obey the one-word limit.
questions.evidence: Although it reflected more sunlight than the original surface, some residents reported uncomfortable glare.
questions.trap: 'Sunlight' is related to the cause but is not the reported problem.
questions.tip: Check both the meaning and grammar of the completed sentence.

questions.question: Complete with ONE WORD from the passage: Older residents particularly appreciated shaded places with _____ to sit on.
questions.explanation: The passage says older residents valued benches where they could rest in shade. The plural noun fits the sentence.
questions.evidence: Older residents often placed particular value on benches where they could rest in the shade.
questions.trap: Do not write 'bench': the evidence and the sentence call for the plural.
questions.tip: Copy the word carefully and preserve its number.

questions.question: The interviews were intended to replace the temperature measurements.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E explicitly states that the interviews added to the measurements rather than replacing them.
questions.evidence: These responses did not replace the temperature measurements; they added information that the instruments could not provide.
questions.trap: Collecting a different type of evidence does not mean the original evidence was abandoned.
questions.tip: Notice how the writer defines the relationship between two methods.

questions.question: Why was the trial extended for another year?
options: A. The first summer produced no usable measurements.
B. The council wanted more evidence about long-term value.
C. Every tree planted in the first year had died.
D. Residents demanded identical designs on every street.
questions.explanation: The council needed to assess value over time, including maintenance, tree survival and usage. A, C and D make unsupported absolute claims.
questions.evidence: It had not yet collected enough evidence to determine which combination of measures offered the best value over time.
questions.trap: 'Not enough evidence' does not mean 'no usable evidence'.
questions.tip: Distinguish limited evidence from the complete absence of evidence.

title: A library of things
content:
A. Most people associate a library with books, but some communities also lend objects that are useful only occasionally. A drill, a carpet cleaner or a sewing machine may spend most of its life unused in a cupboard. Sharing such objects could reduce the need for every household to own one. To explore the practical challenges, consider the following fictional example: a neighbourhood lending project called the Elm Street Library of Things.

B. Before opening, the organisers asked residents which objects they would actually borrow. The answers differed from the organisers' initial expectations. They had assumed that camping equipment would be the most popular category, but cleaning tools attracted more interest. The project began with a limited collection based on the survey. Items were chosen for durability, ease of repair and the availability of replacement parts, rather than simply for the lowest purchase price.

C. Members reserved objects through a website, although telephone reservations were also accepted. Every new member received a short introduction to the borrowing rules. Some tools required an additional demonstration before they could be taken home. A standard loan lasted seven days, and borrowers could request an extension if nobody else had reserved the item. This rule allowed occasional flexibility without making popular objects unavailable for long periods.

D. Returning an object involved more than leaving it at the counter. Volunteers checked whether it was complete and working, using a checklist for each type of equipment. Normal wear was expected, but faults had to be recorded so that an unsafe item would not be lent again. The organisers soon discovered that these checks required more volunteer time than they had anticipated. To avoid rushing inspections, they reduced the number of collection and return periods each week.

E. Borrowing was popular with people who had little storage space, but saving space was not the only reason members joined. Some wanted to try a tool before deciding whether to buy their own. Others valued the chance to ask a volunteer how to complete a small repair. The project later introduced repair afternoons, during which experienced members helped beginners diagnose simple faults. These sessions were intended to build confidence as well as keep useful objects in circulation.

F. The environmental effect was harder to measure than the number of loans. A borrowed drill did not necessarily replace the purchase of a new drill: the borrower might otherwise have borrowed from a neighbour or abandoned the task. Travel also mattered, since a special car journey could add to the impact of a loan. The organisers therefore began asking members what they would have done without the service and how they had travelled to collect an item. Their aim was to understand actual changes in behaviour rather than assume that every loan produced the same benefit.

questions.question: The organisers' survey showed greater interest in camping equipment than in cleaning tools.
questions.explanation: Camping equipment was the organisers' prediction, but the survey showed that cleaning tools attracted more interest.
questions.evidence: They had assumed that camping equipment would be the most popular category, but cleaning tools attracted more interest.
questions.trap: An initial expectation is not the same as the later finding.
questions.tip: Look for contrast words such as 'but' that introduce the actual result.

questions.question: Members could reserve an object without using the website.
questions.explanation: Telephone reservations were accepted, so the website was not the only booking method.
questions.evidence: Members reserved objects through a website, although telephone reservations were also accepted.
questions.trap: The first method mentioned is not necessarily the only method.

questions.question: Complete with ONE WORD from the passage: A standard loan could last for seven _____.
questions.explanation: The text states the standard loan duration directly. 'Days' is the required plural unit.
questions.evidence: A standard loan lasted seven days, and borrowers could request an extension if nobody else had reserved the item.
questions.trap: The possibility of an extension does not change the standard loan period.
questions.tip: Distinguish the normal rule from an exception.

questions.question: Why were collection and return periods reduced?
options: A. Website reservations had become impossible.
B. Fewer residents wanted to borrow objects.
C. Equipment inspections took more time than expected.
D. Volunteers were required to buy replacement tools.
questions.explanation: The checks were taking more volunteer time than anticipated. The schedule was reduced to prevent inspections from being rushed.
questions.evidence: The organisers soon discovered that these checks required more volunteer time than they had anticipated.
questions.trap: A reduction in opening opportunities does not prove that demand fell.
questions.tip: Locate the stated cause rather than infer one from the outcome.

questions.question: Members paid a lower fee if they volunteered at repair afternoons.
questions.explanation: The passage describes repair afternoons but provides no membership fee or discount rules.
questions.evidence: The project later introduced repair afternoons, during which experienced members helped beginners diagnose simple faults.
questions.trap: A sensible reward scheme can seem likely, but likelihood is not textual evidence.
questions.tip: Check whether all parts of the statement, including the fee comparison, are addressed.

questions.question: Complete with ONE WORD from the passage: Repair afternoons aimed to increase beginners' _____.
questions.explanation: The stated personal benefit of the sessions is greater confidence, alongside keeping objects in use.
questions.evidence: These sessions were intended to build confidence as well as keep useful objects in circulation.
questions.trap: 'Circulation' describes the objects, not the beginners.
questions.tip: Match the answer to the person or thing named in the question.

questions.question: Each loan definitely prevented a member from buying a new object.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly says that borrowing did not necessarily replace a purchase. Alternative behaviour included borrowing elsewhere or abandoning the task.
questions.evidence: A borrowed drill did not necessarily replace the purchase of a new drill: the borrower might otherwise have borrowed from a neighbour or abandoned the task.
questions.trap: The absolute terms 'each' and 'definitely' conflict with the qualification 'not necessarily'.
questions.tip: Compare the strength of the statement with the strength of the evidence.

questions.question: What was the main purpose of the questions introduced at the end of the passage?
options: A. To identify the most expensive tools to replace.
B. To assess whether members knew the borrowing rules.
C. To measure how the service changed members' behaviour.
D. To choose a new location for the project.
questions.explanation: The questions addressed alternative actions and travel choices so the organisers could understand actual behavioural changes.
questions.evidence: Their aim was to understand actual changes in behaviour rather than assume that every loan produced the same benefit.
questions.trap: The questions concern the effect of borrowing, rather than operational details such as rules or location.
questions.tip: Use the writer's explicit statement of purpose when one is provided.
